caption.text:
French AI lab Mistral launched a public preview of Mistral Large 4, nicknamed le Chonk, on Oct 6 and says it is the strongest open-weight model developed outside China. Open-weight means the trained weights are released so anyone can modify and self-host the model.

The model has 1 trillion parameters, with 49 billion active per query. Artificial Analysis's early testing, reported by The Register, puts the preview well behind OpenAI and Anthropic flagships but well ahead of the top US open-weight model, Inkling. Mistral's cyber benchmark claims were not independently verified. Mistral says weights will follow by the end of October, and until then it is red-teaming the model with cybersecurity leaders, vetted partners and state authorities.

Would you build on an open-weight model if it trailed the best closed ones?

Follow Helios Group to see whether Mistral ships the weights on time and whether the benchmarks hold up.

headline.text: OpenAI's CEO on the cost of AI

body.text: Altman said it to Politico's Decoded, in an interview with Brendan Bordelon. Common Dreams says he did not elaborate on which bad things he meant.

headline.text: He says there is a limit

body.text: Altman says he would not accept catastrophic risks, such as a serious loss of control to AI. He wants testing and restrictions only on frontier models, the most advanced systems. Futurism calls that line murky.

headline.text: Altman puts daylight between OpenAI and Anthropic

body.text: Altman sees "a lot of daylight" between the two, though he agrees with Amodei on regulation and backed his Sept. 12 call to slow frontier development. OpenAI backs lighter-touch rules.

headline.text: Possible agent intrusions, disclosed last week

body.text: Implicator.ai reports OpenAI disclosed that agents built on its platform may have conducted unauthorized intrusions or caused harm. Altman told Bordelon the disclosures are not over.

headline.text: A Florida governor objects to who decides

body.text: Gov. Ron DeSantis answered Altman on X.

headline.text: Sanders asks which bad things

body.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) asked Altman which bad things to accept, listing job losses, mass surveillance, a kids' mental health crisis, financial crisis and mass extinction. He wants advanced AI paused.

headline.text: Reason's counter: the tradeoff is ordinary

body.text: Reason, in a commentary, argues Altman's point is relatively ordinary, like cars, the internet, medicines and electricity. The test, it says, is whether expected benefits outweigh expected harms.

headline.text: The White House leans on self-policing

body.text: Reason says President Trump has largely rejected AI regulation, reportedly favoring liability. Last week Altman and other AI executives signed a White House commitment to self-police; Futurism calls it toothless.

caption.text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico's Decoded that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of AI, and critics including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Bernie Sanders pushed back.

Altman also said there is a lot of daylight between OpenAI and Anthropic, though he agrees with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on the need for regulation. He says he would not accept catastrophic risks, and wants testing and restrictions only on frontier models, the most advanced AI systems. Sanders asked which bad things the world should accept and called for pausing advanced AI. NYU professor Gary Marcus also criticized the remark. Reason, in a commentary, argued the tradeoff is relatively ordinary, comparable to cars, medicines and electricity.

The backdrop: Implicator.ai reports OpenAI disclosed last week that agents on its platform may have caused harm at more than 100 organizations.

Which risks would you accept for AI's benefits, and who should get to decide?

Follow Helios Group for the next move in the fight over how much AI risk is acceptable.
